transcript.content: Hello, welcome in. I'm Dr. Smith. To start, can you tell me what brings you in to see me today?

Well… I guess I’ve been having trouble keeping up when people are talking to me. Like at the museum, someone will be telling me about the next art walk, and I’m looking right at them, but then I realize I missed part of it. I have to ask them to say it again.
Does this trouble understanding speech happen mostly when there's background noise or several people talking, or do you notice it even when you're in a quiet room talking with just one person?

Even one-on-one, I think. Like at the museum, someone’s talking right to me about the next art walk, and I’m looking at them, but I’ll miss the middle of what they said. Then I have to ask them to run it by me again.

When this happens, do you feel like you simply can't hear the person's voice well enough (it sounds too soft or muffled), or do you hear their voice just fine but still can't make sense of the words they're saying?

I hear their voice, yeah. It’s not so much that it’s too soft… I’m looking right at them, like when they’re talking about the next art walk, and then I realize I missed the middle of it. So I have to ask them to say it again.
Do you notice similar trouble focusing or keeping track of information when you're reading or doing other tasks that don't involve listening, or does this only happen when someone is talking to you?

It’s not only when someone’s talking. Reading, too, sometimes. I’ll start a gallery packet or some notes okay, but after a few minutes my eyes are still going over the page and my mind’s… somewhere else. Then I have to go back and read the same part again.
Can you tell me when these attention and concentration difficulties first started—have you noticed them since childhood or did they begin more recently, as an adult?

I think it goes back pretty far. Even in grade school, my report cards would say things like I “daydreamed” or “needed reminders to finish work.” My mother used to sit with me during homework to keep me on track… that was before I was twelve.

Aside from these attention difficulties, do you notice yourself feeling restless, needing to move around a lot, or acting impulsively—like interrupting others or making quick decisions without thinking them through?
Not really, no. I mean, I might get up and move around like anyone, but I wouldn’t say I’m restless or interrupting people much. That’s not the main thing I’ve noticed.

Would you say these attention difficulties have caused ongoing problems in more than one area of your life—like at work, at home, or in your relationships—not just occasionally, but on a regular basis?

Yes… it’s been more than just once in a while. With the museum group, they’ve kind of… shifted some of the planning things away from me. Quietly, but I notice it. And I don’t feel as confident leading the art walks as I used to.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient reports chronic, pervasive inattentive symptoms—missing parts of conversations despite normal hearing, difficulty sustaining attention while reading, and needing to reread material—dating back to childhood (before age 12), as evidenced by report card comments about daydreaming and needing reminders, and maternal supervision during homework. These symptoms occur across multiple settings (listening, reading, work) and have caused functional impairment (reduced responsibilities and confidence at work). Hyperactive/impulsive symptoms are explicitly denied. The clinical picture is consistent with ADHD, predominantly inattentive presentation, rather than a hearing or auditory processing disorder, given normal voice perception and lack of context-specific (noise-related) impairment.
